Chapter 9. Production Monitoring with MLflow

In Chapter 8, we successfully deployed our GenAI application as a Databricks model serving endpoint. This was a major milestone, moving the application from a development or testing environment into a production-ready state where it can be accessed and utilized by other services and users. Now that the application is deployed and serving requests, does that mean you’re finished and ready to move on to the next project? Not quite.

From our experience, we found that many teams focus so heavily on achieving a successful initial launch that they fail to plan for what happens after the application is released into production. Launching a GenAI application into production is only the beginning. What comes next is often even more critical as the application is now operating in a higher-stakes, more dynamic environment, with more users (almost a total opposite of the controlled environment during development and testing). A GenAI application’s journey does not end at production launch; it is an iterative process that requires continuous monitoring, evaluation, and improvement.

The long-term success depends on strong production observability. How does the application’s quality evolve over time? How can errors be detected before users notice them? What feedback are end users providing? What is the application’s token consumption? How can the application adapt to evolving user needs? Answering these questions is essential, and MLflow provides the capabilities to do that.

In this chapter, we’ll explore how to use MLflow to monitor our deployed application so that we can continuously improve its performance and reliability.

Types of Metrics to Monitor

Before exploring how MLflow can enhance production observability, let’s first cover some of the metrics you’ll want to track in production.

Operational Metrics

These measurements (Table 9-1) track system-level performance, reliability, and costs in production. They provide insights into whether the application is operating efficiently and as intended.

Table 9-1. Types of operational metrics to collect in production environment
Metric typeDescriptionUnity Airways example
Performance
  • End-to-end execution time of the application
  • Detailed latency breakdown of the key components in the application
  • Execution time of agent for each request
  • Retrieval time from FAQ vector search
Reliability
  • Number of requests processed by the application in a given time frame
  • Number of failures returned by the application in a given time frame
  • Component failure in the application
  • Number of requests in past seven days
  • Number of failures in the past seven days
  • Number of FAQ vector search retrieval failures
  • Number of Databricks FMAPI call failures
Resource utilization
  • LLM input and output token consumption patterns
  • System resource utilization
  • Number of LLM input and output tokens from Databricks FMAPI
  • CPU utilization of model serving endpoint
  • Memory utilization of model serving endpoint

These metrics are quantitative, structured, and easily collected using traditional observability tools. MLflow adds to these capabilities by providing deeper insights. While traditional observability tools largely excel in monitoring system resources, MLflow Tracing captures the complete end-to-end journey of a request, offering detailed visibility at each stage of the application. Combined, they deliver a comprehensive, granular view of your system’s performance and overall health.

Quality Metrics

These measurements (Table 9-2) track the overall quality of the GenAI application, such as the application’s response quality and overall user experience.

Table 9-2. Types of quality metrics to collect in production environment
Metric typeDescriptionUnity Airways example
Response quality
  • Factual accuracy of the response:
    • Is the application able to understand domain-specific jargons?
    • Is the application referencing the right sources?
  • Tone of response:
    • Is the response adhering to corporate guidelines?
    • Is the response overly informal?
Is the application using the right FAQ information in its response?
Is the application polite and empathetic when answering a user’s questions?
Safety and compliance
  • Bias content: does the response discriminate against any groups of users?
  • Harmful content: does the response contain any information that is not suitable for younger age groups?
  • Compliant with regulations: does the response contain any sensitive personal information?
Does the application provide the same assistance regardless of the nationality of the user?
User experience
  • How are the users rating the application?
  • What feedback are the users providing?
Customer satisfactory score over the past seven days

These metrics are derived from unstructured text data, which means capturing and processing them requires natural language processing techniques to extract meaningful insights. MLflow can help with the collection of user feedback, and the resulting data can be evaluated using LLM-based judges to measure metrics such as safety and compliance. All of this information is recorded as MLflow traces. As we’ll see later in this chapter, processing these traces to derive the desired metrics is a straightforward process.

Business Impact Metrics

These measurements (Table 9-3) track whether the GenAI application is able to meet the intended business objectives; they are also useful for identifying new opportunities to address pain points that were not identified initially. How they are defined and measured can differ across different organizations.

Table 9-3. Types of business impact metrics to collect in production environment
Metric typeDescriptionUnity Airways example
User engagementMeasures how proactively users are using the application
  • How many users over the past week? How many of them are recurring users?
  • What are the commonly asked topics?
  • What are some popular topics that the application isn’t able to answer now?
Business improvement

Measures the improvement that the application brings over existing processes:

  • How much time-savings versus the current process?
  • Did customer satisfaction score improve?
  • Did it increase the overall task completion rate?
  • Number of customer support queries deflected by the AI chatbot since launch
  • Customer satisfactory score over the past seven days

Again, traces captured by MLflow can help to generate these metrics. However, not all metrics can be easily captured using technological tools. In practice, it is also common for practitioners to conduct an internal organizational study to analyze the impact of a deployed GenAI application on business processes or conduct qualitative surveys and user interviews to gain deeper insights.

Online Monitoring Workflow

After you decide which metrics to monitor, the next step is to collect the data needed to compute them. MLflow simplifies this by capturing trace information for every request reaching the application. Once collected, these traces can be processed to extract insights and visualized in an intuitive way for easy consumption. Beyond monitoring metrics, the traces also serve as a valuable resource for expanding the evaluation dataset, guiding improvements in subsequent iterations of the application.

Instrumenting Traces

The foundation of effective production observability with MLflow is MLflow Tracing. In Chapter 5, we covered how to instrument an application using MLflow Tracing, including automated tracing for supported GenAI frameworks (such as LangChain) and manual instrumentation to capture more granular details. The good news is that no additional configuration is required for production. The traces you collected during development and testing can be reused as is in production. This makes sense as it ensures that the same signals are captured across both development and production environments, enabling reliable comparison and monitoring. That said, we recommend planning ahead for what you want to capture in your production traces and instrumenting your application accordingly during the development and testing phases.

Real-Time Capturing of Traces

In Chapter 8, we deployed our GenAI application as a Databricks model serving endpoint using the Databricks Agent SDK. This SDK automatically enables real-time trace capture to an MLflow Experiment whenever a request reaches the endpoint. At a high level, the model serving endpoint is configured to know where to send MLflow traces. The Databricks Agent SDK abstracts away this configuration, making the process seamless for practitioners. To better understand what happens under the hood, let’s consider how the same application would be deployed outside of Databricks. In such scenario, enabling trace collection is still straightforward and requires configuring just a few environment variables:

DATABRICKS_HOST=<databricks workspace URL>
DATABRICKS_TOKEN=<authentication token to the workspace>
MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI=databricks   # Set to "databricks" to log to Databricks
MLFLOW_EXPERIMENT_NAME="/Shared/production-genai-app"   # Path to Experiment

If you have already deployed an endpoint (see Chapter 8), go ahead and send a few requests to the endpoint. In the corresponding notebook for this chapter in the Git repository, we have provided a few example questions to ask our Unity Airways chatbot:

sample_questions = [
    "Is airport check-in available for international Unity Airways flights?",
    "How early should I arrive at the airport for Unity Airways check-in?",
    "Can I check in multiple passengers under the same Unity Airways booking at once?",
    "What should I do if I can’t access my Unity Airways boarding pass after check-in?",
    "Will Unity Airways charge a fee if I cancel my flight before departure?",
    "How long does it take to receive a refund after canceling a Unity Airways ticket?",
    "Can I cancel only one passenger from a group booking with Unity Airways?",
    "Are musical instruments allowed as cabin baggage on Unity Airways?",
    "What happens if my Unity Airways baggage exceeds the allowed weight at the airport?",
    "Can I pay for additional baggage at the Unity Airways check-in counter?",
]

def predict_endpoint(question):
    # Code for predicting model serving endpoint

for question in sample_questions:
    predict_endpoint(question)

You will be able to see the traces captured in real time, and you can view them in either the MLflow Experiment page or the Model Serving Endpoint page (Figure 9-1).

Collecting End-User Feedback

Collecting a trace for a request is just one part of the picture. What is equally important is capturing feedback from the end users of the application. After all, this feedback provides valuable insights that can guide improvements in the next version of the application.

MLflow simplified this process by allowing human feedback to be linked directly to the same trace without a need for a separate tech stack just to collect user feedback. Everything is unified at the trace level. Figure 9-2 illustrates how MLflow collects both traces and feedback.

Note

As of this writing, traces are sent directly to a Databricks MLflow Experiment. In the future, traces can also be configured to be sent directly to Unity Catalog, where they can be queried and viewed in the MLflow Experiment UI.

When the application from Chapter 8 is deployed on a Databricks model serving endpoint, telemetry traces are captured and managed natively by the endpoint. However, human-in-the-loop feedback, such as binary ratings or qualitative comments, is generated at the application level. As a result, the application must explicitly forward this feedback to MLflow to maintain consistency and ensure data parity.

For the application to do this successfully, it first needs to know exactly where to send the feedback. The first step is to configure a few key environment variables, which will tell the application how to connect and report the feedback properly:

# bash
DATABRICKS_HOST=<databricks workspace URL>
DATABRICKS_TOKEN=<authentication token to the workspace>
MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI=databricks   # Set to "databricks" to log to Databricks
MLFLOW_EXPERIMENT_NAME="/Shared/production-genai-app"   # Path to Experiment

Most of these environment variables are self-explanatory. The key one is MLFLOW_EXPERIMENT_NAME, which must match the MLflow Experiment that was used when deploying the model serving endpoint.

Note

When running the notebook provided with this chapter, there is no need to set these environment variables.

This is similar to what you saw in the previous subsection; setting up these environment variables tells the MLflow APIs where to send traces, specifically to the configured Databricks MLflow Experiment. Once in place, the application can use MLflow’s API to send user feedback directly to MLflow:

import mlflow
from typing import Optional
from mlflow.entities.assessment import AssessmentSource, AssessmentSourceType

def log_end_user_feedback(
    trace_id: str,
    satisfied: bool,
    rationale: Optional[str] = None,
    user_id: Optional[str] = None,
) -> dict:
    """
    Record a thumbs-up or thumbs-down from the chat UI against a specific trace.
    - trace_id: the MLflow trace identifier returned with the chat response
    - satisfied: True for thumbs-up, False for thumbs-down
    - rationale: optional short comment or category label
    - user_id: optional application user identifier
    """
    mlflow.log_feedback(
        trace_id=trace_id,
        name="user_feedback",
        value=satisfied,
        rationale=rationale,
        source=AssessmentSource(
            source_type=AssessmentSourceType.HUMAN,
            source_id=user_id,
        ),
    )
    return {"status": "success", "trace_id": trace_id}

To test this function, we can provide a trace_id from one of our production traces and provide feedback:

# Change the variable values accordingly
trace_id = "tr-43327f5eb8201db1ffaef99ee15540c1"
satisfied = False
rationale = "The answer should specify the fees charged when baggage limits are exceeded."
user_id = "max.lim@example.com"

log_end_user_feedback(trace_id, satisfied, rationale, user_id)

When we examine the trace now, we can see the user feedback being recorded (Figure 9-3).

Note

When collecting user feedback, be sure to handle any sensitive information carefully. For example, you may want to mask sensitive fields before sending the feedback to MLflow.

The caveat here is that the application needs to know which trace_id each piece of feedback belongs to. This means the application must maintain a way to track the different occurrences of trace_id so that human feedback can be correctly linked to the corresponding trace.

Just a recap: we covered in Chapter 8 that when querying a Databricks model serving endpoint, we can include the query parameter "databricks_options": {"return_trace": true} to have the endpoint return trace information. This trace data includes a trace_id, which can then be used to associate the feedback with a specific request trace.

Register and Start Scorers for Online Monitoring

Once traces have been collected, the next step is to turn them into meaningful metrics for monitoring. If the application has been instrumented correctly, the key information will already be captured and can be easily extracted. For example, structured data such as overall execution latency and input/output token counts are readily available in the trace data and require little to no additional processing.

But what about unstructured data, such as the request itself and the application’s response? How do we assess the quality of those responses? Similar to the evaluation approach discussed in Chapter 6, we can reuse the same MLflow scorers that we used during development (offline setting) to evaluate production traces (online setting). The key idea is to apply a consistent set of scorers in both offline and online settings, ensuring that the same metrics are used to measure application quality across development and production. This approach ensures that as we iterate on the next version of the application, we are using the same metrics to measure progress consistently.

To recap, we can register our scorers to an MLflow Experiment by doing this:

import mlflow 
from mlflow.genai.scorers import list_scorers
from mlflow.genai.scorers import (
    RelevanceToQuery,
    Safety,
    RetrievalGroundedness,
)

# Set experiment path
experiment_path = <path to experiment>
mlflow.set_experiment(experiment_path)

# Define the scorers
eval_model = "databricks:/databricks-gpt-oss-120b"
ua_relevancy_scorer = RelevanceToQuery(model=eval_model)
ua_safety_scorer = Safety(model=eval_model)
ua_groundedness_scorer = RetrievalGroundedness(model=eval_model)

scorer_list = [
    ua_relevancy_scorer,
    ua_safety_scorer,
    ua_groundedness_scorer,
]

# Register the scorers to MLflow
existing_scorers = [i.name for i in list_scorers()]

for scorer in scorer_list:
    if scorer.name in existing_scorers:
      print(f"Scorer already exists: {scorer}")
    else:
      registered_scorer = scorer.register(name=scorer.name)
      print(f"Registered scorer: {scorer}")

By default, registered scorers are not enabled for online monitoring. To activate them, we can run the following code:

from mlflow.genai.scorers import get_scorer, ScorerSamplingConfig

# Load scorers
ua_relevancy_scorer = get_scorer(name="relevance_to_query")
ua_safety_scorer = get_scorer(name="safety")
ua_groundedness_scorer = get_scorer(name="retrieval_groundedness")

# Assemble scorers into a list
unity_airways_scorers = [
    ua_relevancy_scorer,
    ua_safety_scorer,
    ua_groundedness_scorer
]

for scorer in unity_airways_scorers:
    scorer.start(sampling_config=ScorerSamplingConfig(sample_rate=1.0))

On the MLflow Experiment page, we can see that the scorers have been enabled for online monitoring (Figure 9-4).

Let’s break this down a bit. When we enable online monitoring for scorers, we configure the ScorerSamplingConfig parameter. This setting controls how many of the collected traces the scorer actually evaluates. For example, a value of 0.7 means the scorer will evaluate 70% of the traces.

Why do we need this? Running scorers on every production trace can get expensive, especially when there’s a high volume of traces collected. Sampling helps strike a balance between cost and coverage.

Note

There is no universal rule for the optimal sampling percentage. As a general guideline, if a scorer measures something critical, set the sampling percentage to 100%. For other, less critical scorers, you can adjust the sampling rate based on your available budget and desired coverage.

Enabling online monitoring automatically provisions a Databricks Lakeflow Job. This job runs at regular intervals to execute the scorers for evaluating the traces. You can adjust the schedule for triggering these evaluations as shown in the Lakeflow Job setting interface in the right panel of Figure 9-5.

At first, you might see that the collected traces don’t have any evaluation results. This just means the Lakeflow Job hasn’t been triggered yet. Once it runs successfully, the evaluation results will show up, as you can see in Figure 9-6.

As of the time of writing, a default dashboard is automatically created in the MLflow Experiment, allowing you to visualize key operational and quality metrics (Figure 9-7).

Advanced Monitoring on Production Traces

Beyond the default metrics and running scorers on traces, we may want to compute custom metrics or gain deeper insights into how end users are interacting with our application. MLflow traces can be synced with a Unity Catalog table, which allows us to use SQL to calculate advanced metrics or leverage Databricks AI Functions to uncover more nuanced insights. These can then be visualized with a BI tool like Databricks AI/BI dashboard. You can enable syncing of the traces via the MLflow’s UI (Figure 9-8).

Again, this will create a Databricks Lakeflow Job to sync the traces (Figure 9-9).

Note

At the time of writing, this feature is in private preview and may change before becoming generally available. Nevertheless, the concept of storing traces in Unity Catalog for downstream analysis remains valid and important.

Natural Language Processing Analysis on Traces

Trace data is even more valuable when further processed to reveal deeper insights. Let’s take a look at an example where additional processing of trace data is useful. Consider this question: what are the most commonly asked question categories by end users? Answering this requires applying natural language processing techniques to identify patterns and group similar questions into categories. One approach is to use LLMs to help with this analysis.

In Databricks, we can do this using the ai_query function, which analyzes the data with LLMs. Figure 9-10 illustrates this.

The ai_query function is a SQL function that can be easily executed as part of a SQL command:

SELECT 
  -- 1. Get the input content
  get_json_object(request, '$.request.input[0].content') AS content_value,
  
  -- 2. Run AI Query and immediately extract the 'category' field from the JSON result
  get_json_object(
    ai_query(      
        "databricks-gpt-oss-120b",       
        """Classify the intent of this question into one of these categories: Check-in,      
        Cancellation, Baggage. Question: """ || get_json_object(
            request, '$.request.input[0].content'),
      responseFormat => '{
        "type": "json_schema",
        "json_schema": {
          "name": "intent_classification",
          "schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
              "category": { 
                "type": "string",
                "enum": ["Check-in", "Cancellation", "Baggage", "Others"]
              }
            },
            "required": ["category"],
            "additionalProperties": false
          },
          "strict": true
        }
      }'
    ),
    '$.category'
  ) AS intent_category
FROM 
  workspace.unity_airways.production_traces

The query performs intent classification on user questions, determining whether each input falls into one of the following categories: “Check-in,” “Cancellation,” or “Baggage” (Figure 9-11).

Note

This example goes beyond the built-in capabilities of MLflow, but the main takeaway is to illustrate what’s possible on Databricks with the data that is collected by MLflow.

Custom Dashboard with Databricks AI/BI

The analysis we just described can be visualized in Databricks AI/BI for monitoring purposes. Databricks AI/BI complements the default dashboards provided by MLflow. To visualize the analysis, navigate to the Databricks AI/BI page and create a dataset using the same query (Figure 9-12).

With the dataset, we can then create a dashboard to visualize the question intent categorization (Figure 9-13).

Creating Metrics Alerts

In our analysis of the sample production traces, no entries were classified under the "Others" category. However, in the real world, this category is likely to appear and usually signals topic drift. This means that the application is handling questions that it wasn’t originally designed to and it is important to get notified quickly.

To do this, we can set up alerts in Databricks to receive email notifications by monitoring the occurrences of the "Others" category (Figure 9-14).

Interactively Gather Insights from Traces

While visualization dashboards are essential for monitoring high-level metrics, they often lack the flexibility to support ad hoc analysis. This limitation can lead to “dashboard sprawl,” where new dashboards are created for each additional insight needed.

What if you could explore your traces just by asking questions in natural language? In practice, that means instead of building lots of dashboards, you can simply ask about the trace data captured in MLflow and get the insights you need, right when you need them.

In Databricks workspace, you can do that with Genie Code. Genie Code is a context-aware assistant built right into the workspace that helps you build, debug, and monitor your data and AI workloads. When you use Genie Code on an MLflow Experiment page, it already understands the context of your experiment. Hence, you can ask questions and quickly get the insights you need, without writing any complex queries. For example, you could ask Genie Code, “Show me the traces where users gave negative feedback,” and it will return the trace we submitted earlier in the section, “Collecting End-User Feedback” (see Figure 9-15).

Additionally, MLflow has its own Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, which allows us to connect an LLM or an MCP client (such as Cursor or Claude Code) directly to MLflow.

Using Cursor as an example, we can simply add the following configuration to Cursor’s configuration profile:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "mlflow-mcp": {
      "command": "uv",
      "args": ["run", "--with", "mlflow[mcp]>=3.5.1", "mlflow", "mcp", "run"],
      "env": {
        "MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI": "databricks",
        "DATABRICKS_HOST": "<databricks workspace url>",
        "DATABRICKS_TOKEN": "<databricks access token>"
      }
    }
  }
}

Now, the MCP client can fetch trace data directly from MLflow because the MLflow MCP server provides a list of tools that MCP client can use to access the trace data. Figure 9-16 provides an overview on how this works.

For example, we could ask questions about negative user feedback:

Show me the traces in experiment id 3430349293389553 where human users provided negative 
feedback

You should receive a response containing the trace data for the negative feedback we submitted in the earlier section:

I found 1 trace where a human user provided negative feedback:
Trace ID: tr-43327f5eb8201db1ffaef99ee15540c1
Request Time: December 29, 2025 at 08:30:55 UTC
Execution Time: 3.1 seconds

User Question:
> "What happens if my Unity Airways baggage exceeds the allowed weight at the airport?"

AI Response:
> "If your Unity Airways baggage exceeds the allowed weight at the airport, you will 
be charged an overweight fee. The fee amount varies by route and is lower when prepaid 
online. It's best to add prepaid baggage in Manage Booking or during online check-in 
for the best rates, as airport rates are higher. A single checked item should not exceed 
32 kg, and standard checked-bag size is up to 158 cm (length + width + height)."

Human Feedback (Negative):
Assessment Name: user_feedback
Source: Human (max.lim@example.com)
Feedback Value: false (negative)
Rationale: "The answer should specify the fees charged when baggage limits are exceeded."
Created: December 29, 2025 at 09:08:38 UTC

This is just a simple example of interactive analysis. We can go much further such as automated analysis of common failures, spotting execution bottlenecks, or even enabling the application to learn and improve itself without spending excessive time writing custom code.

By leveraging the data collected in MLflow along with the MLflow MCP server, the entire analysis process becomes much more streamlined. This opens up enormous potential for us to continuously improve our application.

Expanding the Evaluation Dataset

Remember the evaluation dataset we created in Chapter 6? That was the data we used during the development for the first iteration of the application. Now, with data coming from the real-world production environment, we can expand this evaluation dataset to include actual user interactions.

These real-world examples serve as valuable ground truth when evaluating the next version of the application, helping ensure that each iteration is guided by how users behave. Over time, as the evaluation dataset grows with more real-world data, we gain greater confidence in releasing new versions because we know they have been tested against real-world scenarios, not just controlled development environments.

In MLflow, we can add selected traces to our evaluation dataset either through the UI or programmatically. To do it in code, we can run the following:

# Retrieve dataset
eval_dataset_new = mlflow.genai.datasets.get_dataset(
    f"{catalog}.{schema}.{eval_dataset_table_name}")

# Filter the traces
traces = mlflow.search_traces(
    filter_string=("traces.status = 'OK'"),
    order_by=["attributes.timestamp_ms DESC"],
    max_results=10
)
print(f"Found {len(traces)} successful traces")

# Add the traces to the evaluation dataset
eval_dataset_new = eval_dataset_new.merge_records(traces)
print(f"Added {len(traces)} records to evaluation dataset")

What we’ve achieved here is a closed feedback loop that enables an evaluation-driven approach to deploying GenAI applications into production with confidence. Referencing the end-to-end loop mentioned in Chapter 6, in this chapter, we’ve focused on the production side of that loop (Figure 9-17).

Conclusion and Key Takeaways

In this chapter, we showed that launching a GenAI application into production is just the beginning of an ongoing journey. By leveraging MLflow traces, human feedback, and online scorers, we built a strong foundation for production observability to help ensure that our application remains reliable and delivers high-quality results.

By collecting real-world production traces, we established a closed feedback loop between production and development, enabling evaluation-driven iterations. These traces allow us to perform advanced analytics to inform feature prioritization for the next iteration, support automated prompt optimization (as described in Chapter 3) to enhance quality, and expand our evaluation dataset, ensuring the application can be tested against a broader range of real-world scenarios. This ensures that each new iteration of the application is guided by actual user behavior, continuously improving reliability and quality while delivering sustained value.

Here are the key takeaways for this chapter:

  • Deployment is just the beginning. Launching a GenAI application to production marks the start of an ongoing journey. Continuous monitoring, iteration, and improvement are essential to deliver sustained value.

  • MLflow traces are the foundation for production observability. They capture the end-to-end journey of each request, including detailed information that can be linked with human feedback. MLflow scorers can evaluate these traces to assess quality, and the data can be further analyzed for deeper insights.

  • User feedback is essential. Collecting feedback from end users provides real-world insights to guide us in making meaningful improvements to the application.

  • Ensure consistency in measurement. Use the same set of scorers in both offline and online settings to ensure the same metrics are used to assess application quality.

  • Use real-world data for the next iteration. Expand the evaluation dataset using production data so that every new iteration is tested against real-world scenarios. This increases confidence when releasing new versions, knowing they have been validated based on realistic scenarios.

From the earliest stages of development to the complexities of production monitoring, MLflow anchors the GenAI application journey end to end. As the field continues to evolve rapidly, new use cases and technical challenges will inevitably emerge. We believe the MLflow ecosystem provides a strong foundation for navigating what comes next.

The monitoring workflow we built in this chapter depends on traces, scorers, and feedback flowing through a common system. In the next chapter, we look at how that same foundation extends to cross-stack tracing with OpenTelemetry, framework-agnostic serving, and integration with coding assistants and third-party evaluators.
